1:
Who is addressed they settle almost together. Keil and Delitzsch describe the psalm as a greeting and its reply, the greeting spoken to the priests and Levites who keep the night-watch in the Temple; they note that the antiphon closes the Songs of degrees, standing as a final blessing. Ordinary worshippers cannot be meant, since their tarrying there through the night was only an exception, and the verb rendered stand is the customary word for priestly service. Ellicott makes both points, citing the Chronicler for Levites whose duties brought them there by night; Wesley says it in a line: the servants are those peculiarly so called, the watch the more necessary by night, and to stand is to minister. Calvin allows the objection before dismissing it: some think others than the Levites are intended, and it must be granted that some zealous of the people remained overnight in the Temple, as Anna did — but the close of the psalm shows the penman addresses priests only, since he prescribes the benediction they were to offer for the people.

What the watch consisted of Henry supplies. Some of the Levites stood by night in the house of the Lord to guard its holy things from profanation and its rich things from plunder, and saw besides that neither the fire on the altar nor the lamps went out. These are the men now called on to bless the Lord: thus they keep themselves awake by keeping themselves employed, and redeem time for holy exercises — and how can we spend our time better than in praising God? It would be excellent husbandry, he adds, to fill the vacancies of time with pious meditations, and modest enough to converse with God when we have nothing else to do.

The opening word Clarke and Spurgeon read as a summons. Clarke takes it in the sense of take heed — be upon your guard, you serve a jealous God, provoke him not. Spurgeon hears it as the departing pilgrims' cry to the nightwatch, stirring up the brotherhood to look above them at the night sky and magnify him who made heaven and earth, and lighted the one with stars and the other with his love. Blessing is the characteristic word of the psalm, he says: the first two verses stir us up to bless Jehovah and the third invokes his blessing on the people — let others bless their stars or praise themselves; as for us, we will bless Jehovah. Gill defines the act more soberly, as ascribing greatness to God and giving him thanks for his mercies, and observes that though all men are of right his servants, only good men are so in fact, made willing by divine grace.

The lifting of the hands turns on one word. Clarke reports the versions — in holiness, in holy things with the Vulgate and Septuagint, in the house of the sanctuary with the Ethiopic — and compares Paul on lifting up holy hands. Ellicott reasons the same way: the usual sense would be toward the sanctuary, but since those addressed already stand in it that is unreasonable, so read in holiness. Gill sets Aben Ezra, who takes it of priests lifting hands to bless the people, against Kimchi, who takes it better of hands lifted to God in prayer. Augustine works instead on the courts, which mean the wider spaces of a house: he who stands in the courts is not straitened but enlarged, and remaining in that enlargement a man can love his enemy, since breadth lies in charity and straitness in hatred. On blessing by night he is blunter: it is easy to bless by day, that is in prosperity, and a man should not boast of blessing with his tongue if he curses with his life — Job blessed in a sad night, when all he possessed had been taken away.
3:
Whose voice speaks the last verse is the question, and Gill canvasses three answers before choosing. It is not, as some hold, the priests blessing the people in this form; it may rather be the wish of the servants of the Lord that God would bless the man who had exhorted them to the service, whether one of the priests, or the captain of the temple, or the psalmist himself; but with Kimchi, and this seems to him the agreeable reading, they are the psalmist's own words, promising a blessing from the Lord to those who blessed him, as an encouragement to every one of them to be constant and diligent in that service — so that the clause may be rendered the Lord shall bless thee. Clarke hears the exchange as a leave-taking between the two parties of the psalm: as if the watch had said, we will attend to your orders, go in peace, and may God shower down his blessings upon you. He takes the blessing itself to be the priestly form of Numbers, the Lord bless thee and keep thee, make his face shine upon thee and be gracious unto thee, lift up his countenance upon thee and give thee peace. Wesley leaves the recipient deliberately open — thee, whosoever thou art, who dost faithfully perform the duty here commanded.

What is asked and where it comes from occupy the rest. Gill observes that all blessings come from the Lord, whether spiritual or temporal, and are to be asked of him and expected from him; and he weighs the words out of Zion, which make these blessings of a particular kind, since it is in the church that God blesses his people with his word and ordinances, with his presence, and with communion with himself — wherefore it is good to be there, waiting on him and worshipping him, praying to him and praising him. Clarke reads the maker of heaven and earth as the guarantee of the gift, since he who governs and possesses all things can give every spiritual and earthly blessing. Ellicott notes only that the style is a frequent one in this group of psalms, and sends the reader back to the like phrase in the psalm of the hills.
